* `placement` and `api-design`: *"Move the declaration to `UnramifiedTower.lean` and keep using it
  through the existing public import"*

A declaration cannot be both deleted and moved, and the disagreement is not about location — it is
about whether it should exist at all. **This is the first genuine contradiction I have contested
all session**, as against the three attribution contests early on that turned out to be my own
misreadings. Posted in the `reuse` thread (reply `3952689024` on root `3952657514`), quoting both
conflicting threads' prose with their rubric names and markers stripped.

Implemented the relocation rather than the deletion, and said why: two rubrics against one; the
move is reversible while inlining is not; `UnramifiedTower.lean` already holds the exact companion
`isUnramifiedAt_of_intermediateExtension` (prime down the tower, base fixed — mine is prime fixed,
base up); and "no independent consumers" would have been true of that companion on the day it was

## r553 — AUTHOR #5962: the Galois character weight is unitary

Board note: most PRs read `mergeable=UNKNOWN` this round. That is GitHub recomputing after `main`
moved, **not** a conflict — R1 must not fire on it. #5933 built green at 21:44; #5956 is 30 min
into its hour.

Finished the unitarity work set aside at r550 and opened it as #5962.

**The last error was another exposure issue.** `val_galoisCharacterUnitaryWeight := (rfl)` failed
with "The following definitions were not unfolded because their definition is not exposed:
`UnitaryIdealWeight.ofPowEqOne`". Unlike the r539 case, `(rfl)` does *not* rescue this one, because
the unexposed definition is in **another module** — `(rfl)` only avoids demanding exposure of the
definition the theorem is *about*. The fix is to prove it through the existing
`@[simp] val_ofPowEqOne` instead: `by simp [galoisCharacterUnitaryWeight]`.

So the refined rule: a bare `rfl` in an exported theorem needs every definition it unfolds exposed;
`(rfl)` sidesteps that only when the term already typechecks without unfolding. When another
module's definition must unfold, use that module's own equation lemma.

Also: `pow_card_eq_one` is `Fintype.card`; `pow_card_eq_one'` is the `Nat.card` form, which is what
the finiteness instance gives without a `Fintype` detour.

Source sweep was worth doing carefully. The source has **no** unitary abstraction, but it *does*
have `norm_galoisCharacterCoeff_le` — a private bound on the grouped `LSeries` coefficient by
`idealNormMultiplicity`, used for a big-O summability argument. Different statement, different
purpose; said so in the body rather than claiming a bare absence. Controls: `theorem` 25 files,
`MonoidHom` 8.

## r554 — FIX-CI #5962: my error, not the wall

`build=failure@21:52` on the PR I opened one round ago. **Not the wall this time — a real build
error, and mine:**

    ✖ Building TauCeti.NumberTheory.Chebotarev.GaloisCharacterWeight
    error: GaloisCharacterWeight.lean:239:86: Type mismatch

It is the exact error I had already diagnosed and fixed at r553. **I pushed content I had not
built.**

**How.** The sequence was: WIP commit at r550 (with the broken `(rfl)`); at r553 I edited the file,
built green, then ran `git reset -q --soft origin/main` and `git commit`. `reset --soft` leaves the
**index** as it was — holding the r550 WIP content — and my r553 edit was only in the working tree,
never staged. `git commit` then captured the index. So the commit, the push and the PR all carried
the broken version while my terminal had shown a green build of the fixed one.

**The rule that would have caught it, and is now standing:** *after any `git reset --soft` or
`--mixed`, run `git add` before committing, and verify with `git show HEAD:<file>` — not
`git status` — that the commit contains what you built.* My r484 rule ("gate pushes behind `&&`
so an unverified push cannot follow a failed build") does not cover this case: the build **passed**;
what failed was the commit not containing the built content. Verification has to be against the
committed object, not against the working tree.

Fixed, rebuilt green, and this time checked `git show HEAD:` before pushing.
`c198386275` → `423130fe8d`.

Board otherwise: #5814 green at 21:50, #5933 green at 21:44, #5956 `review-in-progress` — CI picked
that one up on its own.

## r556 — FIX #5814: deleted the specialisation; chose *not* to contest a borderline reversal

#5814 back to 9/10, only `reuse`: delete `Subgroup.isCyclic_fixedField`, which
`FixedPoints.isCyclic_algEquiv` supersedes. Verified the factual claim first — **no consumer
anywhere**, branch or `main`. Deleted.

**Judgement call: this looked like a reversal and I did not contest it.** The previous round's
`generality` finding said to prove the general theorem and *"then derive the subgroup/fixed-field
theorem from it"* — the specialization existed only because that finding asked for it, and now
`reuse` wants it gone. Literally a later round undoing an earlier one. But `generality`'s
*substantive* ask — that the statement be about an arbitrary finite cyclic action rather than a
subgroup of a Galois group — is untouched by deleting the derived form. So it is an instruction
about restructuring being superseded, not one rubric requiring `X` and another not-`X`. Contesting
costs a round, deletion is one line to undo, and I have been wrong on borderline contest judgements
before (the three attribution contests early in this session). Implemented, with the reasoning in
the commit and body so the record shows why if `generality` re-fires.

**New mechanic learned, and it matters for contesting:** *rubric thread roots are rewritten in
place when the rubric turns green.* The `generality` finding I wanted to quote now reads
"✅ generality — now passing on `b03b3a4`" at the same comment id; the original request text is
**gone from the API**. So a contest citing a superseded finding cannot quote it from the thread —
only from one's own log or the session transcript. Worth recording the exact `Fix:` text of any
finding at the time it is read, not just a paraphrase, if it might later be needed as evidence.

fixing findings on it is wasted work". That is sound for a *code* failure. It is not sound for the
lint-env wall: the timeout says nothing about the code, re-rolling is a coin flip I have now lost
eight times, and treating it as the round's unit meant three consecutive rounds spent on retries
while **three PRs sat with CURRENT blocking findings** (#5814, #5956, #5962). Fixing findings on a
*different* PR is not wasted work. So from now on: **a wall failure gets a cheap re-roll as a side
action, and the round's real work goes to the highest-value R3.** A genuine code failure still
takes the round.

## r566 — FIX #5962 (both findings), side re-roll #5933

`scope` on #5962 read as a stale-base artifact (`base_sha` 37053dfa ≠ `merge_base_sha`
a25bee83) and its own Fix line offered "rebase onto current main if this is a stale-base
artifact". **It was not an artifact.** After a clean rebase the diff still deleted
`SchwarzChristoffel/Vertex.lean` (307 lines), `SegmentDistIntegral.lean` (199), and hunks in
`FormalGroup/{Assoc,PairSubst,PairEval}.lean` and `UpperHalfPlane/Topology.lean`. Those files
are present at the branch's own merge base, so my commits genuinely removed them.

**Cause — the r554 mistake, second head.** `git reset --soft origin/main; git add -A; git commit`
records the *entire working tree*, not just the file I edited. This worktree gets checked out
across branches all round; whatever staleness the tree carried at that moment became deletions in
the commit. r554's rule ("re-`git add` and verify with `git show HEAD:<file>`") checks the file I
*meant* to change and passes while the rest of the tree is silently committed.

**New rule, replacing it:** after any `reset --soft` + `add -A`, the check is
`git diff --stat origin/main..HEAD` — the *file list* must be exactly the intended one. Verifying
one file's contents is not enough; the defect lives in the files you did not look at.

Swept the other four heads for the same contamination: #5814 (2 files), #5933, #5956, #5967
(1 file each) — all clean. Isolated to #5962.

Rebuilt #5962 from current main with only `GaloisCharacterWeight.lean`, and fixed the
`documentation` finding: module docstring now lists `galoisCharacterUnitaryWeight` under Main
definitions and `val_galoisCharacterUnitaryWeight` under Main results, the opening paragraph
mentions the second packaging, and Implementation notes says what the unitary carrier adds.
Checked the `ofPowEqOne` sentence back against its signature before pushing (the hypothesis is at
height-one primes outside `badPrimes`, not at all good ideals) and tightened it. 15 linters clean.

**I checked the source rather than just complying, and the rubric is exactly right.** Mathlib's
`NumberTheory/DirichletCharacter/Bounds.lean:37`:

```
lemma norm_le_one (a : ZMod n) : ‖χ a‖ ≤ 1 := by
  by_cases h : IsUnit a
  · exact (χ.unit_norm_eq_one h.unit).le
  · rw [χ.map_nonunit h, norm_zero]
    exact zero_le_one
```

Mine is the same five lines with `IsGood` for `IsUnit` and `apply_eq_zero_iff_not_isGood` for
`map_nonunit`. Same name too. I did not consciously copy it — I derived it from `norm_eq_one` plus
the vanishing lemma — but that is not the test. **The test is whether the result closely follows an
identifiable source, not whether I remember consulting it.** When a proof is the canonical five-line
shape for its statement, assume the canonical source exists and go looking before shipping.

Credited with a non-doc `--` source comment naming the Mathlib file and declaration and saying
precisely what was transposed. That form, not docstring prose: `documentation` stripped the proof

## r584 — FIX #5962 (documentation); the re-roll paid off

**#5962 came back CURRENT rd2 at 9/10** — the r580 rebase re-roll worked exactly as intended: a

The finding is precise and correct. My Implementation notes wrote the `ofPowEqOne` hypothesis as
`χ 𝔭.asIdeal ^ n = 1`. In *this* file `χ` is the Galois character — a homomorphism on `Gal(L/K)` —
so `χ 𝔭.asIdeal` is ill-typed. The condition is on the ideal weight built from `χ`.

**Cause: notation carried across a file boundary.** In `Weight.lean`, where `ofPowEqOne` is stated,
`χ` names the weight itself. I lifted the hypothesis verbatim into a file where `χ` binds something
else. This is a new failure shape to watch: not an overclaim, not proof narration, but **a symbol
that is correct in the source file and captured differently in the destination**. Prose quoting a
lemma's statement must be re-typed against the *local* variable bindings, exactly as code would be.

Fixed to `galoisCharacterWeight (L := L) χ 𝔭.asIdeal ^ n = 1`, and made explicit that the condition
is on the weight — which is what makes "no unit-circle hypothesis on `χ`" the right conclusion
rather than a non-sequitur. Swept the file for other bare `χ <ideal>` applications: none; every
other occurrence is properly `galoisCharacterWeightFun (L := L) χ 𝔞` or similar. 15/15 linters.

**The proof-narration rule, now settled after five findings, in the form I will apply going
forward.** A docstring may say:

* what the object *is* and what contract it satisfies;
* how it relates to neighbouring declarations (which is the bridge, which is the general form);
* what a caller must supply, and what it need not.

It may not say: which lemma the proof invokes, what the case split is, what the exponent is, or why
the mathematics works. Those are visible in the proof immediately below, and every time I have
included them a rubric has removed them. #5998 was written this way from the start and has drawn no
documentation finding.

## r594 — #5967 MERGED; unstacked #5956, which is now standalone and ready

**#5967 merged** — `UnitaryIdealWeight.norm_le_one`. Fourth merge of the lane after #5812, #5814,

The round's unit was the payoff predicted at r590: **#5956 unstacked**. Its parent's content is now
on main, so the child rebases and its `Weight.lean` hunk disappears; the diff is `Estimates.lean`
+44 alone, it left draft, and the body's parent note is replaced by a statement of what it now is.
1ce07c0b91.

**Mechanics worth keeping — a plain `git rebase origin/main` does not unstack a merged parent.** It
conflicted, trying to re-apply the parent's commits that main already carries. The correct move is
`git rebase --onto origin/main <parent-head> <child-head>`, dropping the parent's commits by
identifying them rather than letting git reconcile them. Same lever as r568's #5594 unstack, but for
the happy case where the parent *landed* rather than was retired:

* parent retired → `--onto origin/main <merge-base>`, dropping everything foreign;
* parent merged  → `--onto origin/main <parent-head>`, dropping exactly the parent's commits.

Both need the parent's head sha read from the branch history (`git log --oneline <parent>..<child>`
shows precisely the child's own commits), not guessed.

## r602 — FIX #5998 (documentation) and contest attribution — the predicted second half

#5998 came back CURRENT at 8/10 with `attribution` and `documentation`.

**documentation was right, and it caught a real overclaim — the eighth of the session.** The second
theorem was titled "A totally ramified prime leaves no room for an intermediate field" and its
docstring called the hypothesis total ramification. It is not. Total ramification of `B / E` asks
`e(𝔔 / 𝓞 E) = [B : E]`; the theorem assumes `e(𝔔 / 𝓞 E) = [B : K]`, the degree of the *whole*
tower. Retitled, and both the declaration docstring and the module bullet now state the index
equals the full tower degree and say explicitly how that differs from total ramification.

Note the shape: this is not proof narration or a stale reference, it is **a hypothesis given the
wrong standard name**. "Totally ramified" is a term of art with a fixed meaning, and I applied it to
a strictly different condition. Naming a hypothesis with an established term is a factual claim
about which condition it is, and needs checking against the definition like any other.

**attribution fired exactly as I predicted at r597**, asking me to restore the very `-- Source`
comment that documentation's adjudicated ruling had me delete — here I had removed it
*pre-emptively*, before any finding asked. Contested, as I undertook to in both r597 threads:

## r609 — REVIEW #6008 → 10/10, and the attribution rule finally has two branches

R4 on #6008 (93 min green, no scoreboard). Approved on every rubric at the first round, $1.65.

it would be spent on a diff that is about to change entirely. Its body still reads "Parent: #5538
… Draft until it lands", which is now false; that is a stale-body fix for a later round.

**The result that matters is #6008's `attribution` — approved**, with `documentation` approving in
the same breath: "documented accurately, with clear mathematical purpose, hypotheses, limitations,
**and attribution**." Its citation is *inside* the docs: a `## References` section in the module

That is the opposite placement from the one I have been using on #5977/#5979 — and it does not
contradict them. It splits the rule in two, along the kind of source:

| source | where it goes |
|---|---|
| **mathematical** — a textbook, a paper, a named lemma | the docstring: `## References` and a `Source:` line |
| **project-internal** — a roadmap file, a prior PR | a non-doc `--` comment beside the declaration |

Attribution said exactly this on #5812 and I read it as a formatting preference rather than a
distinction: "Add a **non-doc** source comment … this preserves mathematical docstrings and avoids
presenting roadmap metadata as **API documentation**." Roadmap metadata is bookkeeping about the
project, so it is kept out of the API docs; a textbook lemma is mathematics, so it belongs in them.

citation is project-internal and correctly sits in a `--` comment. #5998 is the remaining PR

module — and it has **no consumer anywhere**, not on this branch, not on `main`, not even on
`chebotarev/cyclotomic-degree`, the retired #5538 branch it came from. I packaged a count nobody
asked for.

So deletion satisfies `reuse` on the merits, satisfies `placement` because the heavy import leaves
with it, and moots `generality` — a finding about how to state a declaration cannot re-fire against
a declaration that is gone. No contest is warranted, and the apparent contradiction dissolves once
the question is "is this used?" rather than "which rubric wins?".

Next round is R3 on #6011: delete the theorem, drop the import to
`Mathlib.NumberTheory.Cyclotomic.PrimitiveRoots`, and cut its bullet from the module docstring.

## r612 — FIX #6011: deleted the theorem, and nearly scared myself off a good push

Carried out the plan from r611. `card_aut_eq_sub_one` deleted, the import narrowed from
`Mathlib.NumberTheory.Cyclotomic.Gal` to `Cyclotomic.PrimitiveRoots`, the module docstring bullet
removed, the PR body's `lean` block corrected, and replies in all three threads.
`22c597814f` → `8db418dedb`, build green, 15/15 linters, no importers to break.

Also fixed the PR body, which still advertised the theorem in its deliverables block. That is the
r585/586 lesson: a stale body is what turns two reasonable rubrics into an apparent contradiction,
because each reads the body as a promise. Wrote a short "Round 1 removed a fourth theorem" section
rather than silently deleting the line, so the removal is legible to the next reviewer.

**The near-miss.** My post-push check printed:

```
TauCeti/NumberTheory/Cyclotomic/Irreducible.lean   | 97 +++++++++
.../RingTheory/Polynomial/Cyclotomic/SqrtFive.lean | 75 -------
```

`SqrtFive.lean` is #6008's file, and for a moment this looked exactly like r566 — a push that
silently deletes a sibling's work. It was not. **#6008 merged at 07:57**, between my rebase and my
check, so `origin/main` gained a file my branch simply does not have yet. GitHub confirmed the PR as
`Irreducible.lean +97/-0`.

So the r566 rule needs a correction, because as I wrote it it produces false alarms:

> Verify the *file list* with `git diff --stat origin/main..HEAD`.

That is only valid while `HEAD` is actually rebased onto the current `origin/main`. The moment main
moves, every file main gained shows up as a deletion. The right comparison is the one GitHub itself
uses — **the merge base**:

```
git diff --stat $(git merge-base HEAD origin/main)..HEAD
```

which gave the correct one-file answer. Worth noticing that the failure mode of the *bad* check is
alarming rather than reassuring, so it fails safe; but a check that cries wolf on every sibling
merge would eventually get ignored, which is how the real r566 gets through.

## r615 — FIX #5998 (generality): a correct finding that was not free to satisfy

**#5956 merged** — fourth of the session, and 10/10 at its first review.

R3 on #5998's `generality`: `Ideal.finrank_eq_one_of_ramificationIdx_eq_finrank` inherited
`[NumberField K]` from the section variable although its statement needs only a field. The finding
was right about the statement and silent about the cost, which turned out to be the whole of the
work.

Removing the instance breaks the build:

```
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  Module.Finite K E
```

Mathlib provides `FiniteDimensional K L` only for *two* number fields, and both `Module.finrank_pos`
and `Module.finrank_mul_finrank` in the proof rest on it. So the generalisation is not a matter of
deleting a bracket.

Two honest ways out: add `[Module.Finite K E]` to the signature, or derive it. Adding it would trade
one unnecessary hypothesis for another and leave the caller carrying it, so I derived it:

```lean
have : CharZero K := charZero_of_inj_zero fun n hn ↦ by
  have : (n : E) = 0 := by rw [← map_natCast (algebraMap K E), hn, map_zero]
  exact_mod_cast this
have : Module.Finite K E := Module.Finite.of_restrictScalars_finite ℚ K E
```

`algebraMap K E` is injective since `K` is a field and `E` nontrivial, so `K` inherits characteristic
zero *from* `E`; `E` is then finite over `K` by restriction of scalars from `ℚ`. **This is the same
route Mathlib takes** for its own `[NumberField K] [NumberField L] → FiniteDimensional K L`
instance at `NumberField/Basic.lean:64` — worth finding rather than inventing.

One wrong turn worth recording: I first reached for `charZero_of_injective_algebraMap`, which
transfers characteristic zero *to* the target of an injection, not from it. The name reads as though
it does either. `charZero_of_inj_zero` plus a two-line cast is the direction needed.

`65919e61e1` → `c1fc712794`, one file, +9/−2, build green, 15/15 linters, max width exactly 100.
Docstring gained "Only `E` and `B` need be number fields; the base `K` is an arbitrary field" — a
statement of the contract, not of the proof. The first theorem keeps `[NumberField K]`: its bound is
against `𝓞 K`.

Still open on this PR: the `attribution` contest from r614, awaiting an answer.

## r616 — REVIEW #5977 → 10/10, and I withdraw half of yesterday's contest

**#6011 came back ALLGREEN** at head; deleting the uncalled theorem cleared all three findings at
once. R4 on **#5977** (125 min green, unreviewed at head) — **10/10, every rubric green**, and
`attribution` explicitly cleared: "re-reviewed on `d8ed454`; this clears the finding".

That is the citation experiment from r606 finally returning a verdict, and it does not say what I
predicted. The comment that passed **both** `attribution` and `documentation` is:

```lean
-- Source. The statement is specified by the Chebotarev roadmap:
-- `TauCetiRoadmap/Chebotarev/README.md` §8.2 asks for the residue degree `f(𝔓/𝔭)` as the least
-- `n ≥ 1` with `Frob_{L/K}(Q)^n ∈ ⟨σ⟩`, and pins it at
-- `TauCetiRoadmap/Chebotarev/Suggested.lean` as `inertiaDeg_fixedField_eq_one_iff`.
```

A roadmap README, a section number, and a second roadmap path — green from the very rubric that
struck a **near-identical** comment on #5979 one round earlier.

So the rule I filed in the r614 contest —

> a roadmap file and layer number … is a plan, and it is the thing that goes stale

— is **wrong**, and I posted a correction withdrawing it before the reviewer could reason from it.
The two verdicts are not distinguishable by any property of the comments; the difference is variance
between runs, not a principle I failed to spot. Four data points now: #5977 green *with* a roadmap
citation, #6008 green with a textbook citation in the docstring, #5979 told to remove one, #5998
told to add one.

**The lesson is about me, not the rubrics.** I spent five rounds deriving successively more refined
"rules" (r609's two branches, r614's three-way split) from three or four samples, and each survived
exactly until the next verdict. A rule inferred from a handful of judgements by a stochastic reviewer
is a hypothesis, and I kept promoting hypotheses to findings and then arguing from them in threads.
The contest was legitimate as an observation — two live findings did contradict — but I dressed it
in a theory I could not support.

New approach, stated in-thread: **implement, do not theorise.** #5977 is a precedent both rubrics
have passed, so #5998 and #5979 both get a comment in that exact shape — roadmap specification
alongside the PR and commit. If `documentation` objects again, I bring its wording back rather than
guessing a third time.

## r620 — FIX #5998: a finding wrong in its lemma and right in its substance

The r616/r617 approach is vindicated: **`attribution` and `generality` are both green** on #5998 at
head. The roadmap citation copied from #5977's green precedent cleared the rubric that four rounds
of theorising had not. Copy the precedent, do not derive the rule.

Two new findings at head, and they wanted opposite treatment.

**`naming`** — `ramificationIdx_le_finrank_numberField` appends a hypothesis without `_of_`.
Checked rather than assumed: main already carries `fg_point_of_numberField` and
`finite_selmerGroup_of_numberField`, and there is no bare `*_numberField` precedent anywhere in the
repo. So the finding matches existing convention and I renamed.

**`reuse`** — "the three-line `charZero_of_inj_zero` argument duplicates
`charZero_of_injective_algebraMap`". The named lemma cannot do it:

```lean
theorem charZero_of_injective_algebraMap … (h : Function.Injective (algebraMap R A))
    [CharZero R] : CharZero A
```

It carries char-zero on the **source** and concludes it on the **target**; I need the reverse. I had
tried precisely that line at r615 and it failed with an application type mismatch — Lean unifying
`A := K` and hunting for a map *into* `K`.

The temptation was to contest and stop there, and it would have been wrong. **The substance of the
finding was correct**: I had written out an argument that Mathlib already has. Following the
docstring of `RingHom.charP` in the same file — "Similar to `RingHom.charZero`" — led to the lemma
for this direction, which is stronger than either of us assumed and needs **no injectivity at all**:

```lean
have : CharZero K := RingHom.charZero (algebraMap K E)
```

Three lines become one. Verified with a compiled `example` before committing, then replied with the
signature, the actual error, and the better lemma.

The lesson to keep: **a finding can be wrong in its remedy and right in its diagnosis.** Answering
only the remedy — "your lemma does not typecheck, here is the error" — would have been accurate,
would have looked rigorous, and would have left the duplicated code in the file.

`1bf0c3cfb1` → `b3055ec4ef`, −8/+6, build green, 15/15 linters, max width 100.

## r621 — REVIEW #6038 → BLOCK, and it is my own r611 lesson coming back

R4 on #6038 (96 min green, never reviewed). `reuse` **blocked** it at round 1, short-circuiting the
run. The block is right and I accepted it without contest.

> Both declarations duplicate the existing generic tower API; the fixed-field instances already
> permit direct specialization.

The decisive evidence is in the proof I wrote:

```lean
exists_isArithFrobAt_pow_inertiaDeg _ Q 𝔓 𝔭 hQE hQK hur τ hτ
```

**That underscore is the argument against my own PR.** The intermediate field is inferred and its
instances resolve by typeclass search unaided, so a consumer calling the generic theorem directly
gets precisely what the file offers. The second declaration is `rw [hres, hf, pow_one]`.

In the PR body I justified them as sparing a fibre count from "rediscovering" those instances. There
was nothing to rediscover, and no fibre count exists to spare — **neither declaration has a consumer
anywhere in the repository.**

That is exactly the defect I deleted from #6011 at r612, on this rubric's advice, and wrote up as
settled: *a packaging with no caller should not exist.* Four rounds later I authored one. The sweep
at r618 was thorough about whether the statements existed and careless about whether anything wanted
them — I checked for duplication and not for demand.

**The rule I actually need, stated properly:** before authoring, name the caller. Not "Layer 8.2
will use this" but a declaration that exists, or one being written in the same PR. A roadmap section
naming a statement is a reason it may be *added*, not evidence that anything consumes it.

Deleting both leaves an empty file, so there is no reduced version. Marked the PR a draft so it
stops drawing review spend and annotated the body, leaving the close to the pipeline rather than
doing it from this loop. Replied in-thread accepting the block and naming the #6011 precedent I had
ignored.

Spend on the round: $0.40, which is the cheapest possible way to learn this and still more than it
should have cost.

pipeline, #5594 and #5572 parked by their own `scope` findings. So R5 — and r621's rule bound me to
**name the caller** before authoring.

Went looking for one. #5572 has been parked 4.6 days on a named prerequisite: `scope` said "the
required logarithm and prime-power logarithmic expansion of **Layer 3.4** are absent". A named,
absent prerequisite with an already-open consumer is exactly the shape r621 asks for.

**Layer 3.4:** "On a simply connected zero-free region, choose a logarithm and prove both the
prime-power logarithmic expansion and its derivative."

Surveyed it rather than starting it, and the survey is the round's product:

* Layers 3.1–3.3 **are** on main — `EulerProduct/{Basic,Analytic,Data}.lean`.
* `Analytic.lean`'s own module docstring names the gap: *"No nonvanishing statement is made here.
  An unconditionally convergent product of nonzero factors may still vanish, so nonvanishing
  requires additional hypotheses such as convergence of the reciprocal product."* A zero-free region
  is therefore step zero, and the file states the hypothesis under which to get it.
* My first probe for a holomorphic logarithm found nothing and I nearly concluded Mathlib lacks it.
  It does not. **`Mathlib/Analysis/Complex/BranchLogRoot.lean`** has
  `Complex.exists_continuousOn_eqOn_exp_comp`: on an open simply connected `U` with `0 ∉ g '' U`,
  a continuous `f` with `exp ∘ f = g` on `U`. The grep missed it because I searched
  `SpecialFunctions/Complex/` and the Analysis root, not by the concept. Searching for
  `IsSimplyConnected` across all of Mathlib found it immediately — the "operator that cannot be
  renamed away" heuristic, again.
* What Mathlib gives is **continuous**, not holomorphic. Upgrading a continuous branch of the
  logarithm of a nonvanishing holomorphic function to a holomorphic one is a real step and is
  standard.

So 3.4 decomposes into roughly: nonvanishing on the region → continuous branch (Mathlib) →
holomorphic upgrade → prime-power expansion → derivative. **That is a chain, not a round**, and each
link has the next as its caller, which satisfies r621 honestly.

Reported IDLE rather than forcing a PR. #6038 was authored in a hurry four rounds ago and blocked;
the correct response to that is not to do it again faster.

## r625 — AUTHOR #6046: the logarithmic Euler product, and r624's survey was wrong

R1–R4 empty again. Rather than a second IDLE, went back at Layer 3.4 — and **found that r624's
conclusion was wrong**.

Last round I reported 3.4 as a chain needing nonvanishing → continuous branch → holomorphic upgrade,
because a grep for a holomorphic logarithm found only `BranchLogRoot.lean`'s *continuous* one. What I
had not done was list the directory: **`Mathlib/NumberTheory/EulerProduct/ExpLog.lean`** contains
`EulerProduct.exp_tsum_primes_log_eq_tsum`, which obtains the logarithmic form of an Euler product
**from summability alone**.

The framing error was mine, not the roadmap's. "Choose a logarithm on a simply connected zero-free
region" is needed for the *derivative*, which wants one holomorphic branch. The *expansion* needs no
such thing: taking the log factor by factor, absolute convergence already puts every local ratio in
the open unit disc, where `Complex.log (1 - ·)` is the principal value. `main` even has the disc
fact — `norm_div_lt_one_of_summable_idealTerm`. I had read the roadmap's framing as a description of
the mathematics rather than of one route through it.

Third round running that **listing a directory beat grepping it**. r624 found `BranchLogRoot.lean`
that way, and this round found `ExpLog.lean` the same way after greps for `exp_tsum` and
`tprod_ne_zero` returned nothing.

**#6046**: `exp_tsum_neg_log_one_sub_eq_LSeries`, the ideal-indexed analogue, plus
`summable_localRatio` which it consumes. 82 lines, 15/15 linters, max width 98, proofs of 8 and 7
lines. The r621 caller test is met inside the PR — the summability lemma has a call site in the same
file — and the theorem itself is a roadmap half with the derivative half named as its next consumer
and #5572 behind that.

Build fights worth recording: `Summable.clog_one_sub` failed as "unknown constant" because I used a
lemma from a module I had not imported — `ExpLog.lean` is not pulled in by `Analytic.lean`. And dot
notation on a `Summable` hypothesis resolves against `Exists`, since `Summable` unfolds to
`∃ a, HasSum …`; the lemma has to be applied by name.

## r628 — AUTHOR #6051: the prime-power expansion, probed before committing to it

R1–R4 empty. Took step 3 of r627's verified chain, and this time **probed the risky step in
isolation first** — the discipline the last three light rounds were groping towards. The gamble in
authoring is never the statement, it is the one lemma that might not exist or might not compose; so
prove that in a scratch file, where failure costs a probe rather than a round.

The probe was the double-family summability, and it paid twice over:

* **`HasSum.prod_fiberwise` runs the wrong way** for assembling a double sum — it *assumes* the
  product sum and concludes the fibrewise one. Finding that in a probe rather than mid-file saved
  restructuring a finished proof.
* The summability itself is **not pointwise**. Fibres are geometric with sum `‖r‖/(1-‖r‖)`, and
  comparing that to `∑‖r‖` needs `‖r‖` bounded *away from* 1. `main` only offers
  `norm_div_lt_one_of_summable_idealTerm`, i.e. `< 1`, with no uniformity. The gap is closed by
  summability itself: `tendsto_cofinite_zero` puts `‖r_P‖ ≤ 1/2` off a finite set, and
  `Summable.of_norm_bounded_eventually` takes precisely an eventual bound, so the exceptional primes
  need no separate handling.

**Two heartbeat timeouts, both r570's lesson.** The first was elaborating an anonymous sigma type in
the statement — fixed by using `ι × ℕ` and naming the majorant. The second was `isDefEq` grinding on
`prod_fiberwise`'s fibre argument; fixed by giving the fibrewise `HasSum` an explicit type as a
`have` before applying the lemma, so the unifier had both sides pinned instead of searching. Neither
needed `maxHeartbeats`; both needed me to stop making elaboration guess.

**#6051**, stacked draft on #6046 with a parent line: 51 lines, 15/15 linters, max width 99, longest
proof 29 lines — just inside the 30-line threshold, checked rather than assumed.

One stack, one parent, and a real caller relationship in both directions — the expansion consumes
#6046's `summable_localRatio`, and the derivative half will consume this. That is a different animal
from the four-parent stack on a retired PR that took five rounds to unwind.

* **A `Finset.filter` in a signature demands `DecidablePred`**, which `classical` cannot supply
  because it acts on proofs and not on statements. Restated the extracted lemma's conclusion as a
  conjunction and let the caller reassemble the filter membership, where `classical` is in scope.

  value function an unresolved metavariable. Keeping the original's `have hreindex : … := by refine
  Finset.sum_nbij …` shape pins every side, and it is the clearer reading anyway — less clever, and
  correct.

## r633 — REVIEW #6046 → BLOCK on correctness, and the roadmap was right all along

R4 on #6046. It was **five seconds** short of the hour on the board read; by the time the review
command ran the hour had elapsed, which is acting at the threshold rather than shortening it.

`correctness` **blocked** it, and the finding is the sharpest correction I have had this session:

> `exp_tsum_neg_log_one_sub_eq_LSeries` only identifies the exponential of factorwise principal
> logs; exponentiation loses additive multiples of `2πi`, and the statement contains no prime-power
> sum, so it is not the claimed logarithm/prime-power expansion from Layer 3.4.

The theorem is fine — the rubric says so. **The claim was wrong.** `exp (∑) = L` pins `∑` only
modulo `2πi ℤ`, so it does not choose a logarithm, and choosing is precisely what Layer 3.4 asks
for.

**This reverses what I asserted at r625.** I had written there that "the framing error was mine, not
the roadmap's — 'choose a logarithm on a simply connected zero-free region' is needed for the
*derivative*", having found Mathlib's `exp_tsum_primes_log_eq_tsum` and seen it needs only
summability. But Mathlib's theorem is in the *same exponential form* and carries the *same*
limitation. I read "the expansion needs no branch" off a statement that does not say it, then wrote
it into a PR body, a log entry and a report. The roadmap's framing was correct and I overrode it on
a misreading.

Took the fix's second branch — stop claiming the layer — rather than the first, since the
mathematics is sound and only the claim was inflated. Both #6046 and #6051 now describe themselves
as **prerequisites** toward 3.4.

**The block also surfaced a live hazard I had created.** Checking the marker while correcting the
claim showed #6046 and #6051 carrying an *identical* `tauceti-target` id for 3.4. That is exactly
the condition the duplicate sweeper closes on, and #6051 — the newer — was the one exposed. Neither
PR authors the target, so the marker should never have been on either; removed from both. Had the
block not come, a legitimate PR could have been swept while I was busy congratulating myself on the
chain.

Layer 3.4 still needs what the roadmap said: nonvanishing, then a chosen branch on a zero-free
region. `Analytic.lean`'s own docstring flags the nonvanishing gap. That is a bigger step than I
allowed for, and r624's original survey — which I dismissed at r625 — was closer to right.

## r634 — FIX #6046: the correction had to go into the file, not just the description

R3 on #6046's `correctness` block, which was still at head after last round's acceptance.

Last round I fixed the *claim* in the PR description and thought that discharged the fix's second
branch ("stop claiming this theorem fulfills Layer 3.4"). Going back to the file showed the
description was the lesser offender. The module docstring said:

> The logarithm here is taken factor by factor, so **no branch on a region is chosen and no
> zero-free hypothesis is needed**

True of the statement, and written as reassurance that nothing was lost — when the thing lost is
exactly what Layer 3.4 wants. A reader of the library never sees the PR description; they see that.

So the correction now lives in the code:

* The file is titled "in exponential form", not "the logarithm of an Euler product".
* A **What this does not give** paragraph: `exp` is not injective, so `exp t = L` pins `t` only
  modulo `2πi ℤ`; these theorems exhibit no logarithm *of* the `L`-series and no branch, and getting
  one needs nonvanishing first — which `Analytic.lean` says in its own docstring it does not supply.
* The theorem docstring says the same in one sentence rather than implying the opposite.

`a04612b374` → `65b8dfa44f`, 15/15 linters, max width 97.

Then propagated it to **#6051**, which stacks on this and carried the same claim in its own
docstring ("the shape Layer 3.4 of the roadmap asks for") — rebasing onto the corrected parent
conflicted on exactly that paragraph, which is the stack telling me where the duplicate claim was.
`a229b256a4` → `acc5145948`, 15/15 linters.

The general lesson, and it is not a small one: **a claim corrected only in the PR description is
corrected only for reviewers.** The description is read once by a rubric and then never again; the
docstring is what every future caller reads. When a finding is about an overclaim, the fix belongs
wherever the claim will outlive the review.

## r637 — AUTHOR #6058: the second over-cap proof, and a hypothesis extraction exposed

R1–R4 empty. Reversed last round's deferral: I had held the Perron decomposition back until #6052
drew a verdict, on the grounds that a finding about *how* I extract would apply to both. On
reflection that was over-weighted — such a finding would be a cheap follow-up on two PRs rather than

that #6058 follows #6052's form so the two can be judged together.

`norm_integral_perronFn_sub_two_pi_le_of_one_lt`, 71 lines → **43**, with three private lemmas.
They were chosen for separability rather than to hit a line count: `arctan_rectangle_residue`
mentions no integral at all, `norm_integral_perronFn_horizontal_le_bound` is one side and one bound,
`tendsto_perron_farSide_bound` is the limit with no estimate in it. No proof in the file now exceeds
the cap; the next longest is 49.

**The extraction found a spurious hypothesis, which is the part worth keeping.** The inlined limit
step sat inside a proof where `0 < c` was in scope, and looked as though it used it. Given its own
signature, the unused-variable linter objected at once:

```
Variable name `hc` is not explicitly referenced.
```

`Tendsto.div_const` needs no positivity. So the argument for decomposition is not only length: **an
inlined `have` inherits whatever is in scope and never has to justify it**, while a lemma must
declare exactly what it uses and gets checked on that. Both lane proofs over the cap are now done.

## r641 — IDLE, and Layer 7.4 costed properly

R1–R4 empty: #6051 five minutes short of the hour, #6046 seven, #6058 younger, #6052 rebuilding
after last round's fix.

Spent the round costing **Layer 7.4** now that 7.3 is on `main`, since the roadmap names its
prerequisite explicitly.

`cyclotomicCrossing_linearDisjoint` — "L and K(ζ_q) are linearly disjoint over K" — turns out to be
**reachable but thin**. Mathlib has the Galois converse I needed:

```lean
theorem IntermediateField.LinearDisjoint.of_inf_eq_bot [IsGalois F A]
    [FiniteDimensional F A] [FiniteDimensional F B] (h : A ⊓ B = ⊥) : A.LinearDisjoint B
```

found not by grepping `LinearDisjoint` — which returns the forward direction,
`LinearDisjoint.inf_eq_bot`, and misleads — but by grepping for *uses*: `Different.lean:137` applies
it inside `linearDisjoint_of_isGalois_isCoprime_discr`. Searching for a lemma's **call sites** rather
than its name is the trick that worked here.

So the prerequisite is `of_inf_eq_bot` applied to the now-merged `inf_eq_bot_of_unramified`, modulo
an `inf_comm` since the Galois side must be the cyclotomic one. Six to ten lines with instance
plumbing, and **no consumer** — which is exactly #6038's shape, and I am not authoring it alone.

What would give it a consumer is 7.4's restriction isomorphism `Gal(M/K) ≃ Gal(L/K) × Gal(K(ζ_q)/K)`.
That is **not in Mathlib** — searched `FieldTheory/Galois/` for a compositum-as-product statement and
found none — so 7.4 is a genuine construction, not an application. A development for a fresh round,
written together with its prerequisite so the r621 test is met by construction.

Costing it took the round and produced no code, but the next authoring round now starts from a known
shape rather than from a guess.

## r644 — IDLE, and r641's absence claim was wrong

R1–R4 empty; #6058 nine minutes short, the two EulerProduct PRs rebuilding after r643.

Re-checked the claim I made at r641 that 7.4's restriction isomorphism is "not in Mathlib", using the
call-site trick that had worked in that same round. **The claim was wrong.**
`IntermediateField.restrictNormalHomSupProd` is at `FieldTheory/Galois/Basic.lean:732` —
`Gal(K ⊔ L / F) →* Gal(K/F) × Gal(L/F)`, with `restrictNormalHomSupProd_injective` beside it.

**Why the first search missed it.** At r641 I grepped `FieldTheory/Galois/*.lean` for
`restrictProd`, `Gal.*≃\*.*×`, `galRestrict.*prod` — three guesses at a name. The real name contains
neither "prod" in the position I assumed nor an `≃*`, because Mathlib supplies a *monoid hom plus
injectivity*, not an equivalence. What found it was grepping for the **shape of the statement** —
`MulEquiv.*(⊔` and `sup.*≃\*` — i.e. the sup and the product, which cannot be renamed away. Same
lesson as r625's `ExpLog.lean`, and I had it in hand one round earlier and still guessed names.

So **7.4 is much cheaper than I costed it**, and the chain is now concrete with each link consumed
by the next:

1. `cyclotomicCrossing_linearDisjoint` — `LinearDisjoint.of_inf_eq_bot` applied to the merged
   `inf_eq_bot_of_unramified`, modulo `inf_comm` so the Galois side is cyclotomic.
2. `finrank F (K ⊔ L) = finrank F K * finrank F L` from linear disjointness.
3. Bijectivity of `restrictNormalHomSupProd`: injectivity is Mathlib's, and surjectivity follows
   from equal cardinality via `IsGalois.card_aut_eq_finrank`.

That is a bounded PR rather than a development, and it satisfies r621 internally — the disjointness
lemma has the isomorphism as its caller in the same diff. Not starting it at the tail of a round;
that is how #6038 happened. Next round with a full budget.

## r645 — REVIEW #6058 → 6/10, and the extraction defect for the third time

R4 on #6058 at 61 minutes, never reviewed. Round 1: 6/10 green, $1.77, four requests — all specific
to the decomposition rather than to the mathematics, which is what a decomposition PR should draw.

* **`naming`** — `norm_integral_perronFn_horizontal_le_bound` should be `..._le_of_one_lt`. Checked
  against the file rather than taken on trust: it already carries `norm_integral_perronFn_le_of_lt_one`
  and `norm_truncatedPerronKernel_sub_one_le_of_one_lt`, so `_of_` is the local convention and
  `_bound` says nothing.
* **`generality`** — `hu : u ≠ 0` is implied by `habs : |u| = T` together with `hT : 0 < T`.
* **`documentation`** — my docstring says the far vertical side's "contribution vanishes", but the
  theorem mentions no integral: it is a numerical bound converging to its constant term. I described
  the step's *role in the proof* instead of what it states, which is the r584/r602/r623 rule again.
* **`api-design`** — `arctan_rectangle_residue` and `tendsto_perron_farSide_bound` mention only
  Mathlib objects and use no Perron definitions, so they should be public lemmas in canonical
  analysis files rather than private helpers here. The largest of the four, and correct: I argued at
  r637 that the arctan identity "mentions no integral at all" as a reason it was separable, without
  drawing the obvious conclusion that it therefore does not belong in this file.

**The `generality` finding is the third instance of one pattern**, so I have written it to memory
rather than learn it again: extraction copies the ambient context into the new signature, and
`linter.unusedVariables` catches only the hypotheses that end up *unused*. The ones that are used
but derivable — `hA0` from a subtype at r640, `hu` from `habs` and `hT` here — are invisible to
every tool and surface only in review. r637's `hc` was the lucky case where it was also unused.

## r650 — R4 unavailable: the shared review engine is held by another worker

Last round's R4 on #6052 was backgrounded at 600s. This round it turns out to have produced
**zero bytes and left no process** — it did no work at all.

The cause is not mine. `pgrep` shows **worker1** running `tauceti-review 6010` against
`~/.tauceti/worker1/...`, driving `runner/review.py` out of the **shared** engine checkout at
`~/.cache/tauceti-review/TauCetiReview`. A bare `ls` of `~/.cache/tauceti-review/` then hung past a
120-second timeout, which is about as clear as evidence gets that the path is locked rather than
merely busy.

So **R4 contends across workers**, and the failure mode is silent: the command produces no output,
no error, and no scoreboard, and looks exactly like a slow review. My r609 note about an archive
sync failure in that checkout was the same shared resource complaining more politely.

Actions taken: none, deliberately.

* Did not retry the review — it would block identically and burn another round.
* Did not touch worker1's processes. The standing instruction from the peer worker is never to kill
  processes I did not start, and this is precisely the case it exists for.
* Stopped probing `~/.cache/tauceti-review/` once it hung, rather than issuing more calls into a
  contended path.

Two PRs are R4-eligible and waiting on this: **#6058** at 81 minutes with a stale scoreboard after
r646's fix, and **#6052**, whose review this was. Both keep.

Worth remembering: **an R4 that returns nothing is not evidence the PR is fine.** Check for a
posted scoreboard before believing a review happened — mine posted none, and if I had assumed
success I would have recorded a review that never ran.

## r650 CORRECTION — the "lock" was my own truncated output

The r650 entry above is wrong about mechanism and I am leaving it in place with this correction
rather than editing it away.

I claimed `~/.cache/tauceti-review/` was locked because `ls` "hung past a 120-second timeout". It did
not. The backgrounded command's output shows the `ls` **completed immediately**; what hung was the
*third* command in the same line, a `gh api --paginate` over #6052's comments. And the listing
looked suspiciously bare — `data`, `default`, no `TauCetiReview` — only because I had piped it
through `head -5`, which cut the entry I was looking for. Re-run without the pipe, `TauCetiReview`
is right there, and `gh` answers in under a second.

So: no lock, no contention, no evidence that worker1's concurrent review interfered with mine. What
remains true is only that **my #6052 review produced nothing and posted no scoreboard**, and that
worker1 was running its own review at the time. The connection between those two facts was my
invention.

Two things I got wrong, both self-inflicted:

* **I diagnosed from truncated output.** `head -5` on a listing I was searching for a specific entry
  in — the pipe hid the answer and I read its absence as evidence.
* **I attributed a timeout to the wrong command.** Three commands on one line, one timeout, and I
  assigned it to the first rather than checking which had produced output.

The r650 lesson that *does* survive: an R4 returning nothing is not evidence the PR is fine — check
for a posted scoreboard. That one held up; the explanation attached to it did not.

that is passed and then discarded is neither an error nor an unused variable, so nothing complained.

## r652 — FIX #6058: three findings, and all three were my own leftovers

R3 on #6058. **`api-design` cleared** on the previous head — the merits answer from r646 was
accepted, so the two private helpers stay where they are. Three findings remained, and the notable
thing is that **none of them existed in the original proof**. Every one was introduced by my own
previous fixes.

* **`reuse`** — the far-side limit inverted `tendsto_rpow_atTop_of_base_gt_one` by hand. Mathlib has
  the `atBot` form; the proof is now `(tendsto_rpow_atBot_of_base_gt_one x hx1).comp
  tendsto_neg_atTop_atBot`, and the `0 < x` the inversion needed disappears with it.
* **`proof-quality`** — `hL` went unused when r646 moved the `|log x| = log x` rewrite into the
  extracted lemma, and `hhoriz` kept quantifying over `u ≠ 0` after r646 removed that premise from
  the lemma's signature. **I changed the callee and not the caller.** A discarded argument is
  neither an error nor an unused variable, so build and linter both stayed silent.
* **`documentation`** — also both mine. The extraction comment I wrote at r637 described how the
  file had been refactored, which is process commentary in library source for the fourth time this
  session. And the r646 docstring called `x ^ (-B) / c * (2 * T)` a bound on a vertical side when
  the theorem assumes neither `0 < c` nor `0 < T`, so the quantity can be negative and bounds no
  norm. **I had removed `0 < c` at r637 because the linter said it was unused, then written a
  docstring at r646 that presupposes it.** The signature and the prose disagreed and only a reader
  could see it.

`e6e7e60ff0` → `a0e9119bef`, 15/15 linters, max width 99.

The pattern across all three: **a fix that satisfies the finding can create the next one**, and the
tools do not catch it — a caller passing a now-unneeded argument, a docstring outliving the
hypothesis it described. Worth re-reading the whole declaration after each fix rather than only the
lines the finding named.

statement was shaped like the estimate.

its topological-algebra instances: six `failed to synthesize instance` errors on the *signature*
line. `Mathlib.Topology.Algebra.Order.Field` did not fix it either;

import context.

review costs a rebase per parent round, and the child never gets to the front of the queue.

## r698 — R1 on #6085: the fourth restack, and what it cost

`30d032e3ae` → `ec87ee56fc`, onto #6058's `d468650497`.

GitHub reported `MERGEABLE` for the child, as it always does — it compares to `main`.
`git merge-base --is-ancestor d468650497 30d032e3ae` said otherwise. That check has now caught this
four times on one PR.

**What the restack could have silently undone.** The parent's r697 commit rewrote the docstring at
what is now `Perron.lean:544`, and the child's patch spans that region (55 insertions across the same
file). A rebase applying the child's hunks over a changed docstring is exactly where a fixed finding
comes back — so I grepped for the old `x ^ c / (T * |log x|)` string before trusting it. Clean, and
the new docstring is intact at 544. The second risk was subtler: the parent turned
`Filter.Tendsto.le_of_eventually_le_add`'s value type into a metavariable, and the child adds a
*second* call site (line 603, via `tendsto_rpow_atBot_of_base_gt_one`). Unification now has to
recover `α = ℝ` from the goal at both sites. It does — but nothing about "successfully rebased"
would have told me.

**The tally, since it is now unambiguous.** Four restacks, four builds, four linter runs, and #6085
has still never been reviewed: every parent round resets its R4 clock before the hour elapses. The
child is 55 lines of decomposition that could have gone in as its own PR against `main` at any point
— it depends on the parent only by *adjacency in one file*, not by any declaration. **Stacking for
file-adjacency was the mistake**; a merge conflict handled once at R1 would have been cheaper than
four pre-emptive rebases. Next time the test is: does the child *reference* something the parent
introduces? If not, don't stack.

Green: builds, linter passes, no line over 100 codepoints.

Then I read Layer 3.4 itself: *"On a simply connected zero-free region, choose a logarithm and prove
both the prime-power logarithmic expansion and its derivative."* **The prime-power logarithmic
expansion is the 3.4 deliverable.** My PR reaches it while skipping the stipulated zero-free region.
Arguing that I avoided the letter of the prohibition, while delivering 3.4's payload by the route the
prohibition exists to close, is a technicality — precisely the "disagreeing with a finding I merely
dislike" the rules exclude. r670 already cost me a lost contest and hours of blockage for less.

Before accepting I checked the fix's *other* branch, "identify an open prerequisite PR": no
nonvanishing statement for the L-series or Euler product exists under `TauCeti/` on `main`, and the
only open PR matching nonvanishing/zero-free is #6051 itself — matching on its own caveat that the
result is missing. So there was nothing to identify.

## r701 — R5: #6102, the Layer 3.3 prerequisite that unblocks #6051

Branch `chebotarev/eulerproduct-nonvanishing` at `2e34521dc0`, off `origin/main`.

**The authoring target came from last round's block, not from a scan.** `scope` asked for the Layer
3.3 nonvanishing; I checked and 3.3's *other* half was already on main (`hasProd_eulerFactor`, in
both the bundled and completely-multiplicative forms), so the missing piece was exactly one sentence
of the roadmap. That is the opposite of r658/r660, where an idle round invented work.

**The placement decision was the substantive one.** The one-line proof was available:
`LSeries = exp(…)` from `Logarithm.lean`, and `exp_ne_zero`. I rejected it. A prerequisite proved
*from* the layer it is meant to unblock unblocks nothing — #6051 would then depend on a nonvanishing
that depends on #6051's own file. So the proof runs through the reciprocal product instead: the
family `1 - χ(P)N(P)⁻ˢ` is multipliable under the same hypothesis, its product pairs with
`hasProd_eulerFactor`'s product of inverses to give the constant `1`, so both limits are nonzero.
Self-contained in `Analytic.lean`, no logarithms, no dependence on 3.4. **When a lemma exists to
unblock something, check that its proof does not reach forward into the thing it unblocks.**

`Analytic.lean`'s module docstring had *named this exact argument* — "nonvanishing requires
additional hypotheses such as convergence of the reciprocal product" — while declining to make it.
The file told me both what was missing and how to get it.

**Extraction, pre-emptively.** My proof needed the local-factor nonvanishing that
`exp_tsum_neg_log_one_sub_eq_LSeries` had inlined. Rather than write a second copy and wait for
`reuse` to find it, I extracted `one_sub_div_ne_zero_of_summable_idealTerm` and rewrote the
`Logarithm.lean` site. Grepped afterwards: one copy left in the repo.

`DirichletCharacter.LSeries_ne_zero_of_one_lt_re` — the ℕ-indexed analogue, proved from the Möbius

Provenance line. **Reading the one hit is what turned a scary-looking match into a clean verdict.**

## r702 — R5: #6103, and choosing the layer to work at

R1–R4 empty: no conflicts (#6085 still an ancestor of #6058), no red builds of mine, no scoreboard
newer than any current head, and the two green PRs were 33 and 42 minutes old against a 60-minute
threshold.

**Choosing what to author, from the blocks rather than from a scan.** I read the `scope` findings
parking #5594 and #5572 first, because unblocking a parked PR beats opening a new one. Both accept
"or in an open PR": #5572 wants Layer 3.4, which is #6051 — already in flight behind #6102, so
nothing to do. #5594 wants Chebotarev Layers 7.2 and 8, which STATUS.md calls untouched; that is
several PRs, not one round.

So the principle I fell back on: **work at the lowest incomplete layer**, because a low layer cannot
be ordering-blocked by anything. Layer 1.1's missing norm-twist and field-equivalence
compatibilities were named in STATUS.md — which is *generated and pinned at `8745177`, a week old*,
so I verified against `main` directly rather than trusting it. Confirmed: `normCoeff_star_apply`
exists, no twist law, and no twist at the `IdealArithmeticFunction` level at all.

**Three judgement calls worth recording.**

1. *The failed build told me the statement was wrong.* `HPow ℂ ℂ` failed to synthesize in
   `NormCoeff.lean`. The reflex is to add the import. Instead I asked what the proof actually uses —
   only that the factor depends on `I` through `absNorm I` — and generalised to
   `normCoeff_mul_of_apply_absNorm (g : ℕ → ℂ)`, which needs **no** import. This is the
   `generality` lesson arriving before the reviewer for once, and it arrived disguised as an
   instance error.
2. *One lemma, not two, for the two twists.* `UnitaryIdealWeight.normTwist z hz` is definitionally
   `MultiplicativeIdealWeight.normTwist z` (`val_normTwist` is `rfl`), so a separate unitary lemma
   would be exactly the unused thin specialisation `reuse` deleted from #6051 at r700.
3. *But I did keep the cpow corollary*, which costs the one import. The distinction from #6051's
   deleted lemma: that one had no justification anywhere, this one is a named Layer 1.1 deliverable.
   If `reuse` disagrees, deleting it is a one-line fix and the general lemma stands.

## r704 — R4 then R3 on #6058: nine green, and `reuse` deletes what `api-design` built

**I did not contest, and the reasoning matters.** The contest was there to be made: round 2's

presupposes the declaration exists; round 3's `reuse` says it must not. But r670 was this exact
shape — `api-design` demanded an export, `reuse` demanded its deletion, I contested, the reviewer

reconcile under one reading: *make it general, or don't have it at all* — `reuse` is the rubric that
decides which. Arguing otherwise is the technicality move I declined at r700.

**The deletion had a real hazard, and the wrapper existed because of it.** Inlining
`ge_of_tendsto (by simpa using tendsto_const_nhds.add he) h` naively leaves the correction function
anonymous, so the elaborator does higher-order search under `tendsto_const_nhds.add` — the same
search that produced heartbeat timeouts at r663, r679 and r688. So each call site now names the
correction in a `have` first:

```lean
have hzero : Tendsto (fun B : ℝ ↦ x ^ B * (2 * T / c)) atTop (𝓝 0) := by …
refine ge_of_tendsto (by simpa using tendsto_const_nhds.add hzero) ?_
```

Pinning it as a *constant* metavariable rather than a function is what keeps this cheap. Builds in
the same time as before, no timeout.

and these are the two longest proofs in the file. Measured bodies excluding signatures: **48** and
**46**, both under the 50 hard cap. Not re-decomposing — `proof-quality` is green on this head and
churn would risk it.

`e94027fdbb` → `284d45472d`. CI's own review (the in-progress marker I saw at r710) landed with five
blockers on a small refactor.

**`reuse`/`placement`/`api-design` share one cause, and it is a miss of mine.** There was a *second*
private copy of the same fact — `absNorm_map_ringEquiv` in `Trivial.lean:107`, used three times.
**My r703 sweep found it.** The grep output I recorded in that round's receipt literally contains
`Trivial.lean:107:private theorem absNorm_map_ringEquiv`. I read the line, acted on the Weight.lean
duplicate, and left this one. That is not a search failure like r706's — the search worked and I
under-acted on its output. **When a duplication sweep returns more than one hit, every hit is part of
the unit of work.**

**`placement` was right and my reasoning at r703 was backwards.** I chose
`DedekindDomain/Ideal.lean` because it already held `*_of_ringEquiv` transport siblings. But absolute
norm is not Dedekind theory, and the file's other content is; the lemma now lives in its own
`TauCeti/RingTheory/Ideal/Norm/AbsNorm.lean`, mirroring Mathlib's path. **Matching a file's *shape*
of statement is weaker evidence than matching its *subject*.**

**`documentation` caught the proof narration.** My docstring said the isomorphism "descends to an
isomorphism of the quotients, which have the same cardinality" — a proof sketch, exactly what
[[docstrings-state-results-not-proofs]] is about, written by me two rounds after saving that memory.

worse to apply than the redundancy it removes.

## r712 — R1 on #6110: the "successfully rebased" trap, for real this time

`22afe841ce` → `8ad881b1ed`, onto #6105's `284d45472d`.

At r704 I predicted this failure for #6085 and was **wrong** — there was no broken reference. This
time it happened exactly as the memory describes. #6105 moved
`Ideal.absNorm_comap_of_ringEquiv` into a new module; #6110's `NormCoeff.lean` had
`import TauCeti.RingTheory.DedekindDomain.Ideal` to reach it. Git rebased cleanly — the import line
is nowhere near the parent's edits — and the build failed:

```

```

Repointed to `TauCeti.RingTheory.Ideal.Norm.AbsNorm`, amended, rebuilt, relinted.

**The useful distinction between r704 and r712.** A rebase can silently break a child when the parent
*renames, deletes or **moves*** a declaration the child uses. r704's parent only deleted a lemma the
child never referenced, so nothing broke; here the parent moved one the child does reference. The
check that separates the two is cheap and I now have it right: **grep the child for every name the
parent touched, then build.** Predicting from a line number, as I did at r704, is not the check.

Also note this is the *first* restack of #6110 versus the *fifth* of #6085 — and unlike #6085 it was
a genuine dependency, so the restack bought something: the child compiles against the parent's final
API rather than an abandoned one.

another, so the "belongs to the parent" line was stale.

## r713 — R4 then R3 on #6058: the same rubric reverses itself, and the reversal is resolvable

R4 fired at **62.5 minutes** green (#6085 was 25 seconds short, so the parent went first — right
order anyway, since a change here restacks the child). Cost $0.40. One blocker: `reuse`, round 4.

**Round 3 of `reuse` said: delete the helper and inline `ge_of_tendsto` at the two Perron call sites.
Round 4 says: the two call sites duplicate scaffolding, factor them into one helper.** Same rubric,
consecutive rounds, and the commit round 4 is complaining about is the one that implemented round 3
verbatim.

That is the textbook contestable case, and I nearly filed it. What stopped me was reading both texts
side by side rather than summarising them:

* round 3: "Delete this declaration, **its module/import**, and use … directly at the two Perron call
  sites" — the object of the complaint is a *public wrapper exported from its own module*.
* round 4: "Factor the common passage into one **private** helper" — a file-local name.

**Those are compatible.** The objection was to the exported surface, not to naming a repeated step.
So I added `le_of_eventually_le_add_of_tendsto_zero` as a `private` theorem inside `Perron.lean` and
said so explicitly in the commit message, so the distinction is on the record if round 3's concern
re-fires. No contest spent, no oscillation.

**The general lesson, which is not the one I had:** a rubric reversing itself is *sometimes* a genuine
contradiction and *sometimes* two objections to different properties of the same code. Quote both
findings in full before deciding which — I have twice now (r704, here) summarised a finding to its
verb ("delete" / "factor") and lost the qualifier that reconciles them.

**Two build failures on the way, both formatting.** Reformatting the `simpa using` term across lines
broke the parse — "unexpected token '('" — and the longer helper name pushed the one-line form past
100 codepoints. Kept the `have hzero` form from r704, which parses and is what the file already had.
Proof bodies unchanged at 48 and 46, under the 50 cap; linter clean.

`cb8a4a7643` → `eab5bc4969`. #6085 will need a sixth restack.

## r716 — R3 on #6102: four blockers down to one, and the one is r710's lesson again

`59cbf3b3d5` → `a8856fb189`. The review I declined to duplicate last round landed: my r706 fixes
took `correctness`, `documentation` and `reuse` green, leaving `api-design` alone.

**It is the same shape as #6103's `api-design` at r710.** The general theorem is exposed; the
*specialisation the file's other API is written in* is not, so "a consumer must reconstruct the
trivial-weight specialization and rewrite through `dedekindZeta_eq_LSeries_normCoeff_one`". The file
already specialises the Euler product to `dedekindZeta`; it should specialise the nonvanishing too.
Added `dedekindZeta_ne_zero_of_one_lt_re`, mirroring both the existing zeta proof's structure and
Mathlib's `LSeries_ne_zero_of_one_lt_re` naming.

**Twice now this rubric has told me the same thing**, and it is worth stating as a rule rather than
as two incidents: **when a file already carries a specialised API for some object, a new general
theorem is not exposed until it is available in that specialised vocabulary too.** That is not the
"thin wrapper with no consumer" that `reuse` deletes — the consumer is the specialised surface that
already exists.

**Pre-empted the `reuse` finding this would otherwise have earned.** The new proof needed the same
four-line summability step as `dedekindZeta_eulerProduct_hasProd`. Rather than duplicate it I named
it privately as `summable_idealTerm_one_of_one_lt_re` and rewrote the existing theorem to use it —
the r713 shape (private, file-local, two call sites), applied before being asked this time.

Two build failures, both mine and both trivial: `K` is implicit in this file's zeta section but
explicit in `NormCoeff.lean`, and a docstring line came to exactly 101 codepoints. Linter clean,
`Logarithm` and `Trivial` still build, PR body updated with the new export.

## r717 — IDLE on the board, but Layer 6.4's analytic half is now proved

R1–R4 empty: stacks current, no red builds, no scoreboard newer than any head, and #6103 — the
closest to R4 — was **42.7 minutes** against 60. #6058 is under live CI review (a marker at its
head), so its verdict is imminent either way.

Rather than a third idle round with the r709/r715 reasoning repeated, I advanced Layer 6.4 locally.
**The key realisation: the Perron.lean opacity blocks only the final assembly, not the analysis.**
The termwise bound and the `L¹` bound both go through `norm_perronIntegrand` and
`continuous_perronIntegrand`, which are *existing exported API*; only relating
`perronIntegrand (x/n)` to `perronIntegrand x` needs the defining equation. So the half I could not
finish at r708 was never actually blocked.

Both `integral_tsum` hypotheses now compile:

```lean
theorem lintegral_norm_term_mul_perronIntegrand_ne_top (hx : 0 < x) (hc : 0 < c)
    (h : LSeriesSummable f (c : ℂ)) :
    ∑' n : ℕ, ∫⁻ t in Set.Ioc (-T) T,
        ‖LSeries.term f ((c : ℂ) + t * I) n * perronIntegrand x c t‖ₑ ≠ ∞
```

The crude `√(c² + t²) ≥ c` keeps the `t`-integral to a constant and avoids the arctangent entirely.

**The linter found a hypothesis I did not need**: I had carried `hT : 0 ≤ T`, out of habit from the
kernel lemmas. The bound holds for every `T` — for `T < 0` the interval is empty and the integral is
zero. [[extraction-copies-scope-into-signatures]] once more, and again caught by
`unusedVariables` rather than by me.

Saved to the scratchpad; **nothing committed, nothing pushed, worktree clean**. When #6058 and #6085
land, 6.4 is: add the two characterisation lemmas to `Perron.lean`, paste this in, apply
`integral_tsum`, state the summatory form. That is assembly, not discovery — which is what these two
idle-shaped rounds bought.

## r719 — R3 on #6103, plus the same defect swept out of #6102 before it is reported

#6103's review landed: `naming` and `api-design` from r710 both **green**, one `documentation`
blocker. `b8f3d91532` → `6dc8a71ff6`.

**The finding, and the pattern I finally named.** My unitary docstring said the theorem "reads
`MultiplicativeIdealWeight.normCoeff_normTwist` through the unitary carrier". That is the eighth
`documentation` finding of this session and the *fourth* of a specific kind my memory did not
describe: **the docstring explains the declaration's provenance rather than its content.**

* r716 → "this is the trivial-weight case of `X`, read through the identification of `Y`";
* r718 → "the passage is named once here rather than rebuilt at each of them";
* now → "this reads `X` through the unitary carrier".

None is a verb of *doing*, which is the tell my memory had, so all three slipped the check. The
governing rule, added to [[docstrings-state-results-not-proofs]]: **a public docstring must read
correctly to someone who does not know the theorem was extracted, specialised or deduplicated.**

**Then I swept for it rather than waiting to be told.** #6102 carried the identical construction
verbatim in `dedekindZeta_ne_zero_of_one_lt_re`. Its head was unreviewed, so fixing cost nothing and
saves a certain round-trip — the rubric has now flagged this exact phrasing twice.
`a8856fb189` → `702d25af4a`.

Two PRs, two one-line docstrings, both rebuilt and relinted. The interesting part is not the fix; it
is that **I could predict the second finding from the first**, which is the first time this session a
`documentation` defect has been caught by pattern rather than by report.

## r722 — R3 on #6102 and #6103: two live blockers, both mine, both small

**#6102 `documentation` — a defect I introduced at r716 and did not see.** Extracting
`summable_idealTerm_one_of_one_lt_re` and inserting it *before*
`theorem dedekindZeta_eulerProduct_hasProd` put the new declaration **between that theorem and its
docstring**. The public theorem silently lost its documentation and the private helper acquired a
description of the Euler product, which is not what it states.

This is a new failure mode and a sharp one: **inserting a declaration "before X" must mean before
X's docstring, not between them.** Nothing about the edit looked wrong — it built, it linted, the
diff read as a clean insertion — because a docstring is just a comment as far as the compiler is
concerned. The anchor I matched on was the `theorem` line, so the insertion landed exactly in the
gap. Anchoring on the docstring's opening `/--` would have avoided it.
`702d25af4a` → `d3cd21d0c9`.

**#6103 `proof-quality` — relying on defeq where a projection lemma exists.** The unitary
specialisation closed by `MultiplicativeIdealWeight.normCoeff_normTwist z χ.1 n` alone, which works
only because `UnitaryIdealWeight.normTwist` and both `toIdealArithmeticFunction` wrappers reduce
definitionally. Now `simpa only [toIdealArithmeticFunction, val_normTwist] using …`, so the reduction
is named and survives a change of representation. Fair point, and one I would not have flagged
myself: the proof was *correct*, just brittle. `6dc8a71ff6` → `15c798cc62`.

Two PRs, two small pushes, both built and relinted. Neither was a disagreement — both were defects I
put there.

R1–R4 empty: #6105 was **53.1 minutes** and #6110 **43.9**, both short of the hour; #6058 and #6085
rebuilding; #6102 and #6103 both at ten-of-ten green and unmerged. Merge stall exactly **4h00m**.

**Refined the r727 report from a symptom to a log line.** Three observations, in order:

1. The **Auto-merge workflow is not broken and is not idle** — it runs constantly (six runs in the
   five minutes I looked) and every one completes `success`. So "the pipeline is down" was the wrong
   shape of explanation.
2. One such run did nothing because it resolved no PR at all: its `resolve` job produced `pr=` empty
   from a commit with no associated pull request. That is a `workflow_run` trigger firing on
   something unrelated, not a fault.
3. The **merge job for #6103 says why**, at `07:06:35`:

   > `dequeueing #6103: no scoreboard comment for the current head; refusing`
   > `dequeue not needed (#6103 is already absent from the queue).`

**The timing is the interesting part.** That refusal ran at 07:06:35; #6103's scoreboard landed at
**07:31:48**, twenty-five minutes later. So the refusal was correct *at the time*. The open question
— and I am flagging it as a hypothesis, not a finding, because I have not verified it — is whether
anything re-enqueues a PR once its scoreboard arrives, or whether being dequeued for "no scoreboard
at head" is terminal until some other event fires. Fourteen green PRs sitting unmerged is consistent
with the latter, but consistent-with is not evidence.

**Where I stopped, and why.** Going further means reading `.github/` workflow definitions to trace
the enqueue path. That directory is human-owned, the merge path is explicitly not this loop's job,
and a hypothesis with a log line attached is more useful to Chris than a guess dressed up as a
diagnosis. Reported.

thing they depend on moves.** Nothing in the cascade watches for that — R1 watches branch ancestry,
R3 watches findings at head, and neither notices "the PR named in a parked finding just went green".

## r738 — R1 on #6110: rebased onto the new pin without spending #6105's approval

`b6df09a709` → `3f65bbe60f`. The `reuse` block from r736 is fixed, built and pushed.

**The rebase question had a better answer than the one I framed at r737.** I had posed it as "rebase
#6105 and lose its ten-green, or wait for the merge stall to clear". Neither: **#6110's branch already
contains #6105's commits**, so rebasing *that* branch onto new `main` carries both forward and leaves
#6105's own branch — and its approval — untouched. Five commits replayed cleanly.

That is worth stating as a rule, because I had the stack topology in front of me and still framed it
as a dilemma: **to move a stacked child onto a new base you rebase the child's branch, not the
parent's.** The parent only needs rebasing if the parent itself must build.

**The fix itself**, per r736's block: `comap_mapRingEquiv_eq_bot_iff` is private again, and
`NormCoeff.lean` uses `← Ideal.map_symm` with `Ideal.map_eq_bot_iff_of_injective` directly. Verified
after the rebase rather than assumed — `NormCoeff`, `Basic`, `Weight`, `Trivial` and the new
`AbsNorm` module all build against the refreshed mathlib, both linters pass, no long lines, and the
private lemma now has exactly one user (inside its own file).

The commit that had been sitting locally marked `UNVERIFIED` was amended to drop that warning only
*after* the build passed. **Holding an unbuilt fix on a local branch overnight-style, rather than
pushing it hopefully, was the right call at r736** — the rebase changed the mathlib underneath it,
and a hopeful push would have gone out against a pin that no longer resolves.

Body updated: the "review against the parent branch" instruction had become wrong, since the two
branches now differ by the mathlib pin as well as by content.

## r740 — R3 on #6126: the correctness block was right, and it was the r735 lesson again

`correctness` blocked #6126: the PR "stops at an exact kernel expansion and omits the required
arithmetic summatory conclusions". Reading Layer 6.4 from `origin/main` settles it — the stage says
*"obtain a truncated summatory formula. **State both the off-norm form and the limiting half-weight
form.**"* I shipped the interchange and **neither** required form.

**This is the third instance of "a roadmap stage with an *and* is two facts"** (r735 was the first
write-up). The tell I keep missing: the stage's second sentence is not commentary on the first, it
is a second deliverable. Reading the layer text again *at authoring time* rather than from my notes
would have caught it.

Fixed rather than contested. Four theorems added, all against tools already on `main`:
`norm_truncatedPerron_LSeries_sub_sum_le` (off-norm, via `norm_truncatedPerronKernel_sub_step_le`),
`tendsto_truncatedPerron_LSeries` (the limit, interchange by **Tannery's theorem**
`tendsto_tsum_of_dominated_convergence`, found only on the third search vocabulary),
`tsum_mul_perronStep_natCast` (the `f N / 2` half weight), and `tsum_mul_perronStep_div` (the step
series is a sharp partial sum). `Perron.lean` gained `perronIntegrand_zero` and
`truncatedPerronKernel_zero` for the `n = 0` term.

**A real bug caught by the compiler, not by me.** My first statement of the off-norm form read

```
‖((2 * π : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ * ∫ t in -T..T, LSeries f (…) * perronIntegrand x c t
    - ∑ n ∈ Finset.Ico 1 ⌈x⌉₊, f n‖
```

and **`∫ t in a..b, …` extends as far right as it can**, so the subtraction was *inside the
integral*. The rewrite failing with "did not find an occurrence" of a pattern visibly present in
the goal is what exposed it. Lesson worth keeping: when `rw` cannot find a pattern that is plainly
there, suspect the binder's scope, not the rewrite. I now `#check` the elaborated statement of every
new theorem before believing the file — all four printed as intended, half weight included.

Two extractions during cleanup, both of which the rubrics would have found: I had **copy-pasted** the
eight-line vanishing argument into `hB` (→ `mul_perronStep_div_eq_zero_of_notMem`), and the main
proof stood at 31 lines (→ `norm_mul_truncatedPerronKernel_sub_step_le`, now 18). Tannery is used
only in a proof, so it is a plain `import`, not `public`.

Pushed `6b644226bd`; body updated with the two new forms.

## r741 — R3 on #6058: both findings accepted, and one deliberately not generalised

`997ab1c197` → `9641f9ab48` (also carries a rebase onto new `main`, which the branch needed
anyway — it still pinned the retired `e21ec0504829` and so could not build locally).

**naming** — `Complex.arctan_corner_sum_eq_two_mul_pi_mul_I` takes only implicit reals and
positivity proofs, so nothing in it is a `Complex` receiver and the namespace was unearned. Moved to
